traveler: Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti (Abu 'l-Qasim Maslama al-Majriti al-Qurtubi)
title: The Meridian Moved West: Mayrit, the Tables of Cordoba, and the Book That Was Not His
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mayrit, birth on the Manzanares
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is given as circa 950 in the biographical tradition and no source fixes a month or day
stops.campa: On the Manzanares, at the edge of the Marca Media, stands a small Umayyad fortress-town called Mayrit: a wall, a mosque, a garrison watching the road north toward the Christian counties. Here, around the middle of the tenth century, a son is born to Ahmad, and is given the name Maslama. The town keeps no record of the house, the quarter, or the day. What it gives him is the word he will carry for a thousand years: al-Majriti, the man of Mayrit, and nothing besides.
suggested_refs: The excavated Umayyad wall of Mayrit beside the Cuesta de la Vega, Madrid, and the fortress footprint under the Palacio Real

stops.name: Mayrit, the road south and no return
stops.date_confidence: inferred from his floruit; neither the date nor the route of his departure is attested
stops.campa: Mayrit is a garrison, not a school. Whatever the boy learns of number and the sky he learns from men passing through, and what he wants next lies nine days' ride south, where the caliphs keep the largest library in the western world. He goes, in his youth, and the road is not written down. No source records him ever coming back. The town that named him keeps his nisba and nothing else: no house, no teacher, no return, only the direction in which he left.
suggested_refs: The Madrid-Cordoba corridor of the Marca Media, the frontier road system of the tenth-century caliphate
sources: Gap stated: no source consulted records a return to Madrid or the circumstances of the move

stops.name: Cordoba, arrival in the caliphal city
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the year of his arrival is not recorded
stops.campa: He comes into the seat of the Umayyad caliphs of al-Andalus, the largest city in western Europe: markets, paper, water, and a court that buys books the way other courts buy horses. Al-Hakam II reigns. The full name Maslama will be recorded under, Abu 'l-Qasim Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Faradi al-Hasib al-Majriti al-Qurtubi al-Andalusi, holds both cities inside it, the one that bore him and the one that claimed him. Al-Faradi is the divider of inheritances, al-Hasib the reckoner. The names are job descriptions.
suggested_refs: The tenth-century madina of Cordoba, its bridge, mosque and alcazar, as reconstructed from excavation

stops.name: Cordoba, the Great Mosque and the new mihrab
stops.date_confidence: attested for the building works (961-976, the mihrab expansion completed 971); Maslama's presence in the mosque is inferred, not documented
stops.campa: The Great Mosque is being enlarged. Al-Hakam II pushes the prayer hall south toward the river and sets into its wall a mihrab of marble and gold mosaic, the tesserae and the craftsmen for it sent from the Byzantine east. Under the forest of doubled arches the sciences are taught alongside the law. A man who can compute a qibla, an inheritance share, or the hour of a prayer is useful to the building itself. Maslama's Cordoba is this room, and the arithmetic the room requires.
suggested_refs: The mihrab and maqsura of al-Hakam II's expansion of the Great Mosque of Cordoba, completed 971
sources: General architectural history of the Mezquita de Cordoba; the Byzantine mosaicists are attested in the standard accounts, not verified this session

stops.name: Cordoba, the Alcazar and the caliph's library
stops.date_confidence: attested for al-Hakam II's reign (961-976); no source places Maslama inside the library
stops.campa: Beside the mosque stands the caliphal Alcazar, and inside it al-Hakam's library. His agents buy in Damascus, Baghdad, Constantinople, Cairo, Mecca, Medina, Kufa and Basra; a committee of Muslim and Mozarab Christian scholars sits translating Greek and Latin into Arabic. Later accounts give the shelves hundreds of thousands of volumes. No chronicle of that court names Maslama among its ornaments. A school of exact science needs exactly these shelves, and nothing puts him at them.
suggested_refs: The library of al-Hakam II and its translation committee, the documentary base of Andalusi exact science
sources: Gap stated: the source itself notes al-Majriti's absence from the standard account of al-Hakam II's court

stops.name: Madinat al-Zahra, the palace-city on the slope
stops.date_confidence: attested for the site's occupation under al-Hakam II; Maslama's presence there is not attested
stops.campa: Six kilometers west of the city, in the first foothills of the Sierra Morena, the caliphs have built a second city: Madinat al-Zahra, terraced in three levels down the slope, with a reception hall of translucent marble and a basin of mercury said to throw light around the walls when a servant sets it swinging. Power sits here; Cordoba works. No source puts Maslama on these terraces. The patronage that pays for a library and a corps of translators is decided in this house.
suggested_refs: The Salon Rico of Madinat al-Zahra and its reported mercury basin, excavated site west of Cordoba
sources: General historical geography of Madinat al-Zahra; the mercury basin is a traditional report, not verified this session

stops.name: Alexandria, Ptolemy flattens the sphere
stops.date_confidence: traditional, second century CE; background stop, Maslama never travels here
stops.campa: Eight centuries before, in Alexandria, Claudius Ptolemy writes a short treatise on how to draw the sphere of the heavens flat: the Planisphaerium, the geometry of stereographic projection, the proof that circles on a sphere stay circles when they are cast onto a plane from the pole. The Greek is lost. An Arabic version survives. Inside that proof is the instrument that will let a man hold the turning sky in his hand and read the hour off the edge of it.
suggested_refs: Ptolemy's Planisphaerium, surviving only in Arabic and in the Latin made from the Arabic
sources: Standard history of Ptolemy's works; not independently verified this session

stops.name: Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi computes the Sindhind
stops.date_confidence: attested to around 820; background stop, no travel by Maslama implied
stops.campa: Two centuries earlier, in the round city on the Tigris, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi compiles a set of astronomical tables under the Abbasid caliphs: the Zij al-Sindhind, positions of sun and moon and planets, drawn from Indian and Persian and Greek material and computed for the meridian of Baghdad. Every number in it assumes one particular horizon. Carried west, the tables will be right about the heavens and wrong about the hour, and somebody will have to do the arithmetic again.
suggested_refs: The Round City of Baghdad, Madinat al-Salam, and the Abbasid translation establishment

stops.name: Cordoba, the school of exact sciences
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the school's founding is attested, its date is not, and its address is unrecorded
stops.campa: In Cordoba he gathers students and teaches them the exact sciences: astronomy, geometry, the making and use of instruments, the arithmetic of tables. There is no institution behind it and no endowment, only a master and a circle. Ibn al-Saffar comes to it, and Ibn al-Samh, and Abu al-Hakam al-Kirmani. From this room the organized study of number in al-Andalus is dated, and every one of these students will outlive both the master and the caliphate that housed him.
suggested_refs: The Cordoban majlis of al-Majriti, known only through the careers of the men who came out of it

stops.name: Cordoba, the Planisphere and the Almagest
stops.date_confidence: inferred to within his career; the work is attested, the year is not
stops.campa: Maslama takes part in correcting the Arabic Planisphere and improves the existing Arabic renderings of the Almagest, Ptolemy's thirteen books on the motion of the heavens. The projection stops being a curiosity of Greek geometry and becomes a workshop procedure, a way of ruling brass. His students will build the instruments and write the manuals. The theory of the astrolabe enters al-Andalus as something teachable rather than as something inherited.
suggested_refs: Maslama's notes on the Arabic Planisphaerium, transmitted with the text into Latin

stops.name: Cordoba, the arithmetic of a working caliphate
stops.date_confidence: undated within his career
stops.campa: He writes on commercial arithmetic and on taxation, the reckoning of the Andalusi economy: what a merchant owes, what a field yields, how an estate is divided among heirs. He brings surveying and triangulation into the teaching. The same man who moves a meridian also measures a boundary, and a caliphate that runs on land tax and long-distance trade needs both of those from the same man. He is called al-Hasib, the calculator, before he is called anything else.
suggested_refs: The lost treatise on commercial arithmetic and taxation in al-Andalus, known only by report

stops.name: Cordoba, the tables recomputed for a new horizon
stops.date_confidence: contested: one summary of his corpus gives 985, the article on al-Khwarizmi's zij gives around 1000; the conflict is not resolved here
stops.campa: He takes al-Khwarizmi's tables and does the work over for a different sky. The Persian calendar dates in them are converted to the Hijri, the meridian is moved from Baghdad to Cordoba, and errors are corrected where he finds them. What he produces is not a copy but a recension. The Arabic original will be lost so completely that al-Khwarizmi's tables survive only inside Maslama's version of them. The text that reaches Latin Europe is his hand on another man's numbers.
suggested_refs: The Latin Zij al-Sindhind in Maslama's recension, ed. Suter and Neugebauer, the only surviving form of al-Khwarizmi's tables
sources: The conversion of Persian calendar dates to the Hijri is reported from the Suter/Neugebauer edition of the Latin text, not from the articles cited

stops.name: Basra, the epistles of an anonymous fraternity
stops.date_confidence: contested: composition is placed in the mid-tenth century, and scholarship is divided between Basra and Baghdad
stops.campa: In Basra, or in Baghdad, or in both, a fraternity that never signs its own name assembles a set of epistles: arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music, logic, the natural world, the soul and the way back to it. They call themselves the Ikhwan al-Safa, the Brethren of Purity. The Rasa'il are an encyclopedia written as an initiation, and they travel. Within a generation of their compilation the epistles are being quoted at the far western end of the Arabic-reading world.
suggested_refs: The Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa, fifty-two epistles by an unnamed brotherhood

stops.name: Cordoba, a book quoting the Rasa'il while he is still a child
stops.date_confidence: contested: Hamdani's terminus ante quem of 954-960 rests on quotations inside the Ghayat al-Hakim, a text whose own date and authorship are disputed
stops.campa: Somewhere in al-Andalus, between 954 and 960, a book is being written that quotes the Rasa'il. The book is the Ghayat al-Hakim, and its author does not name himself. It quotes them closely enough that a modern scholar can date the reading. This is the earliest hard evidence of the Brethren's epistles in the far west, and it is a date, not a person. Whoever is reading the Rasa'il in those years, Maslama ibn Ahmad is a boy of four to ten, has not left Mayrit, and has no school and no city of his own.
stops.quote: He lays particular stress on quotes from the Encyclopedia dating between 954 and 960 in the anonymous (Pseudo-Majriti) work Ghayat al-Hakim; al-Maqdisi and al-Zanjani are known to have been active in 983...
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Brethren of Purity', reporting Hamdani's argument against the standard identification of the Brethren
suggested_refs: Hamdani's dating argument from the Ghayat al-Hakim's quotations of the Rasa'il
sources: Gap stated: no source traced this session documents Maslama al-Majriti's circle carrying the Rasa'il into al-Andalus

stops.name: Cordoba, the circle edits the Epistles
stops.date_confidence: attested to his circle, undated; the year is placed within his teaching career and is not a source date
stops.campa: When the Rasa'il reach al-Andalus, Maslama's circle takes them in hand: edits them, alters parts, glosses them for readers who did not grow up in Basra. An encyclopedia is not transmitted the way a table is transmitted. It has to be naturalized, and naturalizing it means someone in Cordoba decided what the western copy would say. Which passages were kept and which were dropped is not recorded. What enters Iberian thought is a version made in Cordoba.
suggested_refs: The Andalusi recension of the Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa

stops.name: Harran, the student goes east
stops.date_confidence: attested that al-Kirmani studied at Harran; the years are not fixed
stops.campa: Abu al-Hakam al-Kirmani, born in Cordoba around 970, does what his master never does: he goes east. At Harran, the old city on the plain south of Edessa where the Sabians have kept their star religion and their Greek geometry alive under Islam, he studies geometry and medicine. The master reaches Baghdad only through its books and never leaves Iberia; the student goes and looks at the place the books came from. He comes back to al-Andalus with what he learned there, and with a complete copy of the Brethren's epistles.
suggested_refs: Harran and its Sabian astronomers, the eastern school al-Kirmani crossed a continent to reach
sources: Coordinates for Harran are standard geography, not drawn from the sources cited

stops.name: Zaragoza, the complete Epistles enter Spain
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date is not fixed and Zaragoza as the relay point is a recurring claim in secondary literature, unconfirmed by the sources consulted
stops.campa: Al-Kirmani settles in Zaragoza on the Ebro, in the upper march, and it is here that the complete Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa are credited with entering Spain in full rather than in fragments. Later tradition will hand that credit to his teacher instead. The taifa court of the eleventh century will make Zaragoza a second Cordoba for geometry and philosophy, and it begins with a man who sat in Maslama's circle and then rode east to Harran and back with the books.
suggested_refs: The Aljaferia and the eleventh-century Zaragoza taifa, second home of Andalusi exact science
sources: Gap stated: no source consulted confirms Zaragoza as the relay point

segments.name: The Regent, the Vessel, and the Grave

stops.name: Cordoba, choosing the hour for al-Mansur
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Spanish tradition reports the role, and no source consulted documents direct contact between the two men
stops.campa: Al-Mansur governs. The caliph Hisham II is kept in the palace as a name on the coinage while the chamberlain runs the state and marches an army north against the Christian kingdoms almost every year. Tradition puts Maslama at his elbow for the choosing of hours: which day a campaign should leave, under which configuration of the heavens. The astronomer who recomputes a meridian is also the man asked when to open a war, and in this court those are not two different questions.
suggested_refs: The regency of al-Mansur (Almanzor), 981-1002, and the annual campaigns against the northern kingdoms
sources: Gap stated: al-Mansur's patronage of Maslama specifically is not documented in the sources consulted

stops.name: Cordoba, the egg-shaped vessel
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the experiment is reported from the Rutbat al-Hakim, a work whose attribution to Maslama is disputed
stops.campa: He takes mercury, natural and quivering and free of impurity, and seals it in a glass vessel shaped like an egg, and sets the vessel in a pot over a heat so gentle that he can bear his hand on the outside of it. What comes out is a red powder. He weighs it, and the weight is what it was. Nothing has been added and nothing has escaped: the substance has changed its color and its nature and kept its quantity exactly. Eight centuries before the balance becomes a law, a Cordoban writes down that the balance did not move.
stops.quote: I took natural quivering mercury, free from impurity, and placed it in a glass vessel shaped like an egg. [...] The weight remaining as it was originally.
stops.quote_source: Rutbat al-Hakim, attributed to Maslama al-Majriti, trans. E. J. Holmyard, Isis 6, no. 3 (1924), p. 302; the bracketed cut removes one sentence about the heat of the outer pot
suggested_refs: E. J. Holmyard, 'Maslama al-Majriti and the Rutbatu'l-Hakim', Isis 6.3 (1924), 293-305
sources: Attribution contested: the Rutbat al-Hakim is the same pseudo-Majriti corpus as the Ghayat al-Hakim

stops.name: Cordoba, death without a grave
stops.date_confidence: contested: one article gives 1007, another a range of 1005-1008 CE (398 AH); the conflict is left open
stops.campa: He dies in Cordoba, in his middle fifties, with the caliphate that housed him a few years from collapse. No source records the grave. There is no tomb, no mausoleum, no cult of the site, nothing for a later century to visit; the biographical dictionaries that keep the names of Andalusi scholars keep his without a place to put him. What survives instead is a room full of students and a set of tables computed for the horizon of a city about to burn.
suggested_refs: The Arabic biographical dictionaries of al-Andalus, which record his death and no burial place
sources: Gap stated: no burial site is attested anywhere

stops.name: Cordoba, Ibn al-Saffar keeps the room open
stops.date_confidence: inferred; his teaching in Cordoba after Maslama's death is attested, the years are not fixed
stops.campa: The school outlives him by a generation. Ibn al-Saffar goes on teaching in Cordoba and writes a treatise on the construction and use of the astrolabe that will still be copied and taught in the fifteenth century, four hundred years after his own death. It is a plain manual: how the plates are cut for a given latitude, how the rete turns, how the altitude of a star is taken and the hour read out of it. Nothing in it is original, and every procedure in it is right.
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Saffar's treatise on the astrolabe, in use into the fifteenth century

stops.name: Madinat al-Zahra, the palace-city stripped
stops.date_confidence: attested: the sack falls between 1010 and 1013
stops.campa: Three years after Maslama's death the fitna begins, and between 1010 and 1013 Berber troops sack and burn Madinat al-Zahra. The terraces are stripped, the marble carried off, the palace-city left to be quarried by anyone who wants stone. The caliphate ends in fact before it ends in name. The scholars of Cordoba scatter east and south into the taifa courts, carrying the instruments and the tables with them, which is how the school survives the loss of its city.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Medina Azahara, sacked 1010-1013 and quarried for centuries afterward

stops.name: Mecca, the coordinates of the Kaaba fixed
stops.date_confidence: undated; the source gives the achievement without a year
stops.campa: Ibn al-Saffar determines the astronomical coordinates of Mecca. The school existed for problems of exactly this kind: every mosque in al-Andalus is built facing a point most of its worshippers will never see, and finding that direction is a problem in spherical geometry that requires knowing exactly where both places sit on the globe. The teacher moved a meridian from Baghdad to Cordoba. The student fixes the one place every Cordoban already faces five times a day.
suggested_refs: The qibla problem in Andalusi astronomy: spherical trigonometry in the service of a direction

stops.name: Denia, the disciple dies on the coast
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ibn al-Saffar dies at Denia on the eastern coast, where a taifa court keeps a fleet and a library and takes in the scholars Cordoba can no longer feed. He has left the city, as everyone able to leave has left it. His astrolabe treatise goes on without him, copied out of Arabic into Latin and out of Latin into every European workshop that files a brass plate, and for nine hundred years it will circulate under another man's name, teaching the instrument to people who have never heard of Cordoba.
suggested_refs: The castle of Denia and the taifa court that sheltered Cordoba's dispersed scholars

stops.name: Granada, Ibn al-Samh in Zirid service
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ibn al-Samh, born in Cordoba in 979 and trained in Maslama's circle, ends in Granada in the service of Habus ibn Maksan, Zirid ruler of a new Berber kingdom in the foothills below the Sierra Nevada. He writes on the astrolabe and on the equatorium, the geared instrument that gives a planet's position without computation, for men who cannot do the arithmetic. He dies in 1035, the same year as Ibn al-Saffar at Denia, both of them a long way from the room where they learned.
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Samh's treatise on the equatorium, later translated for Alfonso X's Libros del saber de astronomia

stops.name: Cordoba, the verdict written sixty-one years late
stops.date_confidence: attested: Said al-Andalusi completed the Tabaqat al-Umam in 1068, sixty-one years after Maslama's death
stops.campa: A qadi of Toledo named Said al-Andalusi writes a book classing the nations of the world by what they know. In the chapter on al-Andalus he judges Maslama the best mathematician and astronomer of his time in the country, and dates the beginning of serious scientific work there from his school. Said was born twenty-two years after the man he is ranking died. The verdict that fixes Maslama's place is written by someone who never saw him, out of a memory the school kept for him.
suggested_refs: Said al-Andalusi, Tabaqat al-Umam (1068), trans. Salem and Kumar as Science in the Medieval World (1991)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti', paraphrasing Said al-Andalusi via Salem and Kumar (1991), p. 64
The famous sentence is Wikipedia's paraphrase, not a translated quotation, and is not given here as a quote

stops.name: Toledo, the tables moved again
stops.date_confidence: attested to around 1080; any direct descent from Maslama's Cordoba recension is not established
stops.campa: In Toledo a group of astronomers around al-Zarqali complete a new set of tables computed for the meridian of their own city, and these become the working tables of Latin Europe for two centuries, copied at Paris and Oxford and Marseille and adjusted for each. Whether anything of Maslama's Cordoba recension sits inside them is not established by any source consulted. The habit is what carries: take the tables you are given, and move the horizon underneath them.
suggested_refs: The Toledan Tables and their Latin descendants, the standard European astronomical tables to 1300
sources: Gap stated: no source consulted confirms a direct line from Maslama's tables to the Toledan Tables

stops.name: Bath, the recension turned into Latin
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the transmission literature; the translator is given as presumably Adelard of Bath
stops.campa: In England, on the twenty-sixth of January 1126, a Latin text is finished: al-Khwarizmi's astronomical tables, translated from the Arabic, in the version Maslama made. The translator is taken to be Adelard of Bath, who learned Arabic somewhere on his travels and spent his life arguing that reason outranks authority. Latin Europe receives Baghdad astronomy at second hand and Cordoban astronomy at first, and does not notice the difference for eight hundred years.
stops.quote: The original Arabic version (written c. 820) is lost, but a version by the Spanish astronomer Maslama al-Majriti (c. 1000) has survived in a Latin translation, presumably by Adelard of Bath (26 January 1126).
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Al-Khwarizmi', on the fate of the Zij al-Sindhind
suggested_refs: The Latin Zij al-Sindhind of 1126, the only surviving form of al-Khwarizmi's tables
sources: Wikipedia, 'Adelard of Bath'; the article lists only 'possibly Spain' among his travels, so his route to the Arabic is not fixed

stops.name: Toledo, Alfonso X orders the Ghaya into Castilian
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years 1256-1258; the city is a placement, since the source does not name it
stops.campa: Alfonso X of Castile, who has made Andalusi science royal business, orders the Ghayat al-Hakim turned from Arabic into Castilian between 1256 and 1258. His workshops are already producing star tables, lapidaries, books of chess and dice, all in the vernacular rather than in Latin. Into that program goes a manual of astral magic: how to draw down the power of a planet, what to carve, what to burn, at what hour. It is filed with the astronomy, because at this court it is astronomy.
suggested_refs: The Alfonsine translation workshop and its Castilian scientific corpus, 1250s-1270s
sources: Gap stated: the source does not name the city where the Castilian translation was made

stops.name: Seville, the court that will not sit still
stops.date_confidence: not established: no source consulted fixes the city of the Castilian translation, and the court was itinerant
stops.campa: The court is not fixed. Alfonso moves between Toledo and Seville with his notaries, his astronomers, his Jewish and Muslim and Christian translators, and the work moves with him; a book begun in one alcazar is finished in another. Which of the two cities saw the Castilian Ghaya written down is not recorded anywhere. The Real Alcazar of Seville, rebuilt in the Andalusi manner by a Christian king who kept the craftsmen, is as likely a room for it as anything in Toledo.
suggested_refs: The Real Alcazar of Seville under Alfonso X, one of the itinerant court's working residences
sources: General knowledge of Alfonso X's itinerant court; not verified this session

stops.name: Castile, the Latin book gets a name nobody can explain
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Latin version is made from the Castilian shortly after 1258, without a fixed date
stops.campa: From the Castilian, someone makes a Latin version, and the Latin acquires a title nobody has convincingly explained: Picatrix. The Arabic had meant the goal of the sage. The Latin keeps the doctrine and adjusts it for Christian hands, and under that garbled name it runs through Europe for four hundred years, copied and hidden and denounced and quoted by men who never learn that the sage in the title was a Cordoban whose identity was already in dispute before the book left Arabic.
suggested_refs: The Latin Picatrix, made from the Alfonsine Castilian, with its Christianizing alterations

stops.name: London, Chaucer's astrolabe and a wrong name
stops.date_confidence: attested for Chaucer's treatise (1391) and for Kunitzsch's reattribution (1981)
stops.campa: In 1391 Geoffrey Chaucer writes out a treatise on the astrolabe in English for a ten-year-old boy called Lewis, working from a Latin manual that circulates under the name of Mashallah, the Jewish astrologer of Baghdad, translated by John of Seville. In 1981 Paul Kunitzsch shows that Mashallah did not write it. Ibn al-Saffar did, in Cordoba, in the school Maslama founded. English gets its first instructions for the instrument by way of a wrong name.
stops.quote: Paul Kunitzsch has recently established that the Latin treatise on the astrolabe long ascribed to Ma'sh'allah and translated by John of Seville is in fact by Ibn al-Saffar, a disciple of Maslama al-Majriti.
stops.quote_source: Helaine Selin (ed.), Encyclopaedia of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine in Non-Western Cultures (Springer, 2008), p. 1335, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Astrolabe'
suggested_refs: Chaucer's A Treatise on the Astrolabe (1391) and the pseudo-Mashallah Latin manual behind it
sources: Paul Kunitzsch, 'On the authenticity of the treatise on the composition and use of the astrolabe ascribed to Messahalla', Archives Internationales d'Histoire des Sciences 31 (1981); not opened this session

stops.name: Cordoba, the book dates itself out of his hands
stops.date_confidence: attested from the text's own prologue (348 AH), on an Arabic scan rather than a critical edition
stops.campa: The Ghayat al-Hakim says when it was finished. Its author writes in the introduction that he completed the book in 348 of the Hijra, about 959 of the Christian era, and that he began it after finishing an earlier work, the Rutbat al-Hakim, in 343, about 954. If Maslama ibn Ahmad was born around 950, he was nine years old when the great grimoire of al-Andalus was completed and four when its companion was. The book dates itself out of his hands, and no biography of him mentions it.
stops.quote: the author of the Arabic original states in its introduction that he completed the book on 348 AH, which is ~ 959 CE
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', footnoted to an Internet Archive scan of the Arabic Ghayat al-Hakim, not to a critical edition
suggested_refs: The Arabic Ghayat al-Hakim, prologue with the 348 AH completion date
sources: Contradiction flagged, not resolved: another summary dates the Rutbat al-Hakim to c. 1009, two years after Maslama's death; the Picatrix article puts it before the Ghaya, at c. 954

stops.name: Cordoba, the other Maslama
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death date of Maslama ibn Qasim al-Qurtubi (353 AH)
stops.campa: There is another Maslama in tenth-century Cordoba. Maslama ibn Qasim al-Qurtubi dies in 964, travels in the east, moves among Sufi and Batini circles, and is described by the biographer Ibn al-Faradi as a man of charms and talismans. He fits the Ghaya where the astronomer does not, by his dates and by what his own biographer says he did. Modern scholarship gives up on the name and calls the author Pseudo-Majriti. Two men, one name, one city, and a thousand years of readers who took the famous one.
stops.quote: One recent study in Studia Islamica suggests that the authorship of this work should be attributed to Maslama b. Qasim al-Qurtubi, who died 964 CE (353 AH) and, according to Ibn al-Faradi, was 'a man of charms and talismans'.
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', reporting Maribel Fierro, 'Batinism in Al-Andalus. Maslama b. Qasim al-Qurtubi', Studia Islamica 84 (1996), pp. 87-112
suggested_refs: Maribel Fierro's 1996 Studia Islamica article proposing al-Qurtubi as the author of the Rutbat and the Ghaya
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ikhwan al-Safa', on the two distinct Maslamas
Contested: other scholars hold the Arabic text is simply anonymous

stops.name: Cairo, an alchemist puts a name on the book
stops.date_confidence: attested as before c. 1360, the alchemist's approximate death date; the city is his known base of work
stops.campa: The alchemist Aydamur al-Jildaki writes and compiles in Egypt through the middle of the fourteenth century, and the earliest surviving attribution of the Ghayat al-Hakim to Maslama al-Majriti is his. Four centuries have passed since the book was written. An alchemist looking for an authority finds a mathematician with a reputation for mercury and a school behind him, and from this point the name is attached to the book and does not come off for six hundred years.
suggested_refs: Al-Jildaki's alchemical compilations, carrying the earliest known ascription of the Ghaya to al-Majriti
sources: The placement in Cairo follows al-Jildaki's known Egyptian activity and is not stated in the source consulted

stops.name: Qal'at Ibn Salama, Ibn Khaldun settles the question wrongly
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Muqaddimah's composition in 1377; the castle site is the traditional identification and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: In a castle in the Algerian interior, out of reach of the courts of the Maghrib, Ibn Khaldun writes the Muqaddimah, and in the pages on the occult sciences he names the author of the Ghayat al-Hakim: the astronomer and mathematician Maslama al-Majriti of Cordoba. The greatest historian of the Arabic Middle Ages repeats an attribution made two decades earlier by an Egyptian alchemist. After him, for six hundred years, nobody in Arabic or in Latin thinks to check the arithmetic.
stops.quote: The Arab historian, Ibn Khaldun, in his Muqaddimah, ascribed authorship of Picatrix (referring to the original Arabic version, under the title Gayat al-Hakim) to the astronomer and mathematician Maslama Al-Majriti, who died between 1005 CE and 1008 CE (398 AH).
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', footnoted to Eugenio Garin, Astrology in the Renaissance: The Zodiac of Life (Routledge, 1983), p. 47
suggested_refs: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah, chapter on the sciences of talismans and letters
sources: The location of the Muqaddimah's composition follows the traditional identification with Qal'at Ibn Salama and was not verified this session

stops.name: London, the Picatrix among the English astrologers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the chain of ownership across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the pin stands for England, not a fixed address
stops.campa: One manuscript of the Picatrix passes hand to hand through Elizabethan and Stuart England: Simon Forman the astrologer-physician, Richard Napier the rector who cast horoscopes over his parishioners, Elias Ashmole the antiquary and collector, William Lilly who published almanacs straight through a civil war. Each of them owns in turn a book of Andalusi astral magic written six centuries earlier under a name that was not its author's, and each of them believes he is reading Maslama.
suggested_refs: The British Library Picatrix manuscript and its chain of English occult owners

stops.name: Madrid, a daughter invented in an encyclopedia
stops.date_confidence: attested: no source for Fatima de Madrid is traceable earlier than the Espasa-Calpe entry of the 1920s
stops.campa: A Spanish encyclopedia prints an entry for Fatima de Madrid: astronomer, daughter and collaborator of al-Majriti, corrector of tables, author of a treatise on the astrolabe. No medieval Arabic biographical dictionary knows her. No earlier source of any kind knows her. Arabists including Manuela Marin identify her as a modern fabrication kept alive by repetition, and she goes on being taught in schools and named on plaques in the city that gave her father nothing but a name.
suggested_refs: The Enciclopedia Espasa-Calpe entry of the 1920s, earliest traceable source for Fatima de Madrid
sources: Wikipedia, 'Fatima of Madrid', citing Angel Requena Fraile and Manuela Marin

stops.name: Madrid, a planet named for the man of Mayrit
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 2015 NameExoWorlds results
stops.campa: The Spanish histories call him the Euclid of Spain: a man of one lost treatise on arithmetic, one recension of another man's tables, one disputed grimoire, and a school. In 2015 the International Astronomical Union runs a public vote to name worlds outside the solar system, and a planet circling the star Titawin in Andromeda is given the name Majriti. A frontier town on the Manzanares gave him his name. A thousand years later the name is fixed to a place nobody will ever stand on.
suggested_refs: The NameExoWorlds 2015 designation of Upsilon Andromedae d as Majriti
